title: Conditional Types, Infer Keyword & Template Literal Types
summary: Master type-level programming: conditional types (T extends U ? X : Y), type inference with infer, and template literal type generation.
learningObjectives: Author conditional types using ternary syntax to select types based on generic relationships
Extract inner wrapped types (Promises, Arrays, Return values) using the infer keyword

sections.heading: 1. Type-Level Logic: Conditional Types & The Infer Keyword
sections.content:
TypeScript is Turing complete at the type level: you can perform branching logic, recursion, pattern matching, and string manipulation purely in types.

1. Conditional Types:
Conditional types follow ternary syntax:
`type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;`

When `T` is a union, conditional types distribute automatically over each member:
`type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never;`
`ToArray<string | number>` -> `string[] | number[]`.

2. The `infer` Keyword (Pattern Matching in Types):
The `infer` keyword allows you to declare a type variable to be extracted during pattern matching:

Extracting Promise resolved values (`Awaited<T>`):
```typescript
type UnpackPromise<T> =
  T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : T;
```
If `T` is `Promise<string>`, TypeScript matches `infer R` against `string` and returns `string`!

Extracting function return types (`ReturnType<T>`):
```typescript
type MyReturnType<T> =
  T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
```

3. Template Literal Types:
Introduced in TypeScript 4.1, template literal types allow string manipulation at the type level:
`type Event = 'click' | 'focus';`
`type EventHandler = `on${Capitalize<Event>}`;` -> `'onClick' | 'onFocus'`.

codeExamples.code:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| CONDITIONAL TYPES & INFER PATTERN EXTRACTION                      |
|                                                                   |
|  type Unpack<T> = T extends Array<infer Item> ? Item : T;         |
|                                                                   |
|  Unpack<string[]> ===> Extracts 'string' (Array match!)           |
|  Unpack<number>   ===> Returns 'number' (No match, returns T)     |
|                                                                   |
|  TEMPLATE LITERAL TYPES:                                          |
|  type HttpMethod = "GET" | "POST";                                |
|  type Route = `${HttpMethod} /api/${string}`;                  |
|  const r: Route = "GET /api/users";  // Valid!                    |
|  const bad: Route = "DELETE /items"; // TS Error!                 |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
codeExamples.explanation: Conditional types evaluate ternary branches. 'infer' extracts wrapped internal types.

keyPoints: Conditional types use ternary syntax (T extends U ? X : Y) to perform type-level branching.
The infer keyword extracts component types from complex structures (functions, promises, arrays).
Template literal types generate validated string patterns at compile time.
commonMistakes: Writing deeply nested recursive conditional types without termination base cases, causing compiler limits.
Forgetting that conditional types distribute over union types unless wrapped in tuples ([T]).

sections.heading: 2. Production Event Handler Map with Template Literal Types
sections.content: In event-driven UI systems, generating strongly typed handler names (e.g. `onUserCreated`, `onOrderShipped`) from raw event names ensures developers never misspell callback names.

codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates using template literal types for naming contracts and infer to extract resolved Promise types.

keyPoints: infer enables non-invasive type extraction from third-party libraries without needing published type exports.
Template literal types enable strict pattern matching on strings like semantic versioning or route paths.
commonMistakes: Using infer outside the 'extends' clause of a conditional type, which is a syntax error.

exercises.title: Construct an Action Payload Extractor using Infer
exercises.objective: Write a conditional type that extracts the payload type from an action creator function.
exercises.description: Given Redux-style action creators that return `{ type: string; payload: T }`, implement ExtractPayload<T> using the infer keyword to extract T. If the function does not return an action with a payload, it should evaluate to void.
instructions: Pattern match on `T extends (...args: any[]) => { payload: infer P } ? P : void`.
hints: `T extends (...args: any[]) => { payload: infer P } ? P : void`.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: The infer keyword matches the shape of the return object and pulls out the payload type variable.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What does the 'infer' keyword do in a TypeScript conditional type?

options.text: It casts any variable to the 'any' type.
It introduces a type variable within the extends clause to be deduced from the matched type.
It imports an external module asynchronously.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: 'infer' allows you to declare a type variable inside the condition to capture and extract an internal type dynamically.

options.text: Only strings starting with '/users/' or '/posts/' followed by a numeric string (e.g. '/users/42').

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Template literal types combine string unions to form exact pattern-matched string literal types.

recap: Conditional types provide if-else logic at the type level. Use 'infer' to extract internal types from complex signatures, and template literals to enforce string patterns.
